planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings onto a shaded, moss-covered log, stump, or rock face in humid, humus-rich conditions; it roots along trailing stems wherever they touch damp moss, much as it does on tree trunks in its native rainforest.

directions: Sarmienta repens is a small creeping evergreen gesneriad from the cool, perpetually damp Valdivian rainforests of Chile and Argentina, where it grows as an epiphyte or lithophyte on mossy trunks and rocks in deep shade. Slender trailing stems carry small, glossy, fleshy leaves and in summer produce curious tubular orange-red flowers with a flared, almost hooded lip. In cultivation it needs constant humidity, filtered to deep shade, and a free-draining but never-drying mossy medium, making it best suited to a sheltered woodland log or shaded moss-covered wall in mild, humid climates, or a cool greenhouse elsewhere. It resents both full sun and drought, and is propagated readily from stem cuttings kept moist until rooted.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall and leave outdoors to stratify over winter; transplant seedlings or potted divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich, constantly moist soil in dappled woodland shade.

directions: Omphalogramma vinciflorum is a Primula relative from damp alpine meadows and open coniferous woodland edges of the Himalaya and southwest China, forming a low rosette of soft, hairy leaves that is topped in late spring by large, violet-blue, funnel-shaped flowers held close to the ground on short stalks. It is a classic choice for the cool, humid woodland or alpine house, demanding year-round moisture, cool summer temperatures, and rich, leafy soil that never dries or waterlogs. Grow it in part shade beneath deciduous cover where snow or mulch insulates the crown in winter, and avoid any hot, dry spell during the growing season, which this plant cannot tolerate. Propagation is almost always from fresh seed, since the plant resents root disturbance once established.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted crowns in fall into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil beneath deciduous trees; established clumps flower very early the following spring before the forest canopy leafs out.

directions: Synthyris missurica, often sold as Snow Queen, is a Pacific Northwest woodland native forming a low mound of glossy, rounded, scalloped evergreen leaves that persist through winter. In very early spring, well before most companions stir, it sends up dense spikes of small blue-violet flowers that rise directly from the crown among the overwintered foliage. It thrives in the deep to dappled shade of a conifer or mixed deciduous forest floor, in rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and makes an excellent companion for ferns and trilliums in a native woodland garden. Established clumps are long-lived and spread slowly, and are best increased by division of the crown in fall or by sowing fresh seed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind and hot afternoon sun.

directions: Sinowilsonia henryi is a little-grown, monotypic member of the witch hazel family discovered in central China by Ernest Wilson, valued more for its handsome foliage and curious bloom than for showy flowers. In spring it produces long, pendulous, greenish-yellow catkin-like racemes before the soft, downy, gray-green leaves fully expand, and the foliage often takes on yellow tones in autumn. It is best grown as an understory large shrub or small tree beneath taller canopy trees, in moisture-retentive but well-drained soil, where it is sheltered from harsh sun and wind. Largely a connoisseur's plant found mainly in arboreta and specialist collections, it is otherwise easy and trouble-free once established in a woodland setting.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Start indoors in a shallow pot of fast-draining, humus-rich mix; grow year-round in deep shade with high humidity, moving outdoors to a sheltered shady spot only once nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Petrocosmea sinensis is the type species of its genus, a tidy rosette-forming gesneriad native to shaded limestone cliffs and rock crevices in China, grown for its neat whorl of softly felted, dark green leaves and its late-winter to spring flush of small white flowers marked with a purple-yellow throat. It is a classic subject for an alpine house, cool windowsill, or shaded terrarium rather than the open garden in most climates, needing bright but indirect light, high humidity, and a gritty, humus-rich mix that drains quickly around its crown to prevent rot. Water from below or around the rosette to keep moisture off the fuzzy foliage, and protect from any frost, since it is hardy only in essentially frost-free, humid shade gardens. Propagate by leaf cuttings or by division of offsets from the mother rosette.

planting.note: Establish small divisions directly onto permanently damp, mossy rock, log, or shaded wall in deep shade; it will not survive in open ground or anywhere humidity is not constantly high.

directions: Hymenophyllum tunbrigense is a diminutive filmy fern native to Britain, Ireland, and other high-rainfall parts of western Europe, forming low mats of translucent, one-cell-thick fronds that never develop the waxy cuticle of ordinary ferns and so cannot tolerate drying out even briefly. It grows naturally on shaded, constantly dripping rock faces, mossy logs, and sheltered ravine walls in deep woodland shade with near-saturated humidity year-round. Outside of consistently humid, high-rainfall oceanic climates it is essentially a terrarium or cool-greenhouse subject, but where conditions allow it can be grown outdoors on a permanently damp, mossy log or shaded wall fed by seepage or a misting system. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes and is best left undisturbed once established, since transplanting disrupts its fragile moisture balance.
sources: Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin & Warburg)
